newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Widow of Albania's Hoxha defends husband.
newsitem.headline: Widow of Albania's Hoxha defends husband.

text.p: Nexhmije Hoxha, widow of Albania's Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, released from jail on Friday, defended her husband's repressive rule but acknowledged he made "mistakes".
In an interview published on Saturday in Gazeta Shqiptare daily, Hoxha said her husband, who ruled Europe's poorest country for four decades until his death in 1985, had been vilified by propaganda.
"The biggest mistake was the exaggeration of the class struggle (under communism). I would say the mistakes came from Enver and the lower structures of the party," she said.
"But we were not informed of what happened in reality...Many truths were kept secret from myself and Enver," she added.

During Hoxha's iron rule his relatives held high-ranking posts and enjoyed privileges of which ordinary Albanians could only dream. Religion, private property, travel abroad, and foreign books and films were banned.
The 76-year-old widow insisted her husband was not responsible for banning religion in 1967. "I also think the attitude towards culture was excessive," she noted.

Asked if she and her husband knew about the executions, deportations and torture carried out during their rule, she said: "The issue is exaggerated today. Propaganda does its job...but even today people are tortured in prison."
A popular uprising toppled communism in Albania in December 1990.

Hoxha said Albania was obliged to look to China for assistance after it quit the communist Warsaw Pact and cut ties with the former Soviet Union in 1961 because the West remained indifferent to its plight.

"Europe should have been more flexible," she said. "Enver's principle was the political independence of Albania. But Germany and Britain, with whom we wanted to establish relations, imposed conditions on us that we understandably did not accept."
Albania also terminated its pact with China in 1978 after Tirana criticised Beijing's opening up to the West.

Nexhmije was arrested in December 1991 and sentenced to nine years in jail in 1993 on charges of misappropriation of state funds and abuse of power. An appeals court later raised her term to 11 years, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court.
But her sentence was reduced in a series of amnesties.
Hoxha defended former communist officials sent to jail for ordering the deportation of thousands of anti-communist dissidents and their families to remote areas of the country.
"They only applied the laws of that state," she said.

On her release, Hoxha said one of her first priorities would be to visit the new grave of her husband, first buried in the Martyrs of the Nation cemetery but exhumed in 1992 and reburied in a public plot.
"I do not know where Enver's grave is and I will go and find it. During these five years my mind has not been separated from his name and memories," she said.
Hoxha also hopes to publish her memoirs which she wrote in jail.
